strengths: Identifies a genuine and underexplored gap: existing sparse attention methods for video diffusion are designed for bidirectional models and degrade significantly when naively applied to autoregressive (AR) chunk-wise generation. The motivating toy experiments (Fig. 2, Setting 1-4) and attention-pattern visualizations (Fig. 4) provide convincing qualitative evidence for the two claimed failure modes (chunk-agnostic sparsity and history-forgetting).

The two proposed components (Chunk-Aware Growth for progressive sparsity allocation across chunks, and Hierarchical Sparse Attention for coarse-to-fine frame/block selection) are reasonably well motivated by the empirical observations and are compatible with standard blockwise sparse-attention kernels for practical deployment.

Extensive empirical comparison against five strong sparse-attention baselines (STA, Radial, SVG2, VMoBA, SLA) on two different AR backbones (Self-Forcing, LongLive), with full VBench sub-metric breakdowns provided in the appendix, plus qualitative video comparisons.
The method notably surpasses dense FlashAttention2 baselines in overall VBench score, suggesting the approach captures real redundancy in AR attention rather than trading off quality for speed.

Practical, end-to-end system-level deployment results (FP8 quantization + LightVAE integration) demonstrate a path to real-time generation (19.7 FPS) on consumer GPUs, which is valuable for practitioners.

Ablation studies (component-wise and top-k sensitivity) help isolate the contribution of CAG vs. HSA, and the negligible (~2%) overhead claim for the frame-retrieval step is a useful practical detail.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for Chunk-Aware Growth (Sec 4.1, Appendix B) borrows a generic diffusion-sampling TV-distance bound from prior work (Li et al., 2023) that characterizes standard sampling/score-estimation error, but the paper does not rigorously establish how attention sparsity specifically maps onto the εscore term; the final sparsity-allocation formula (Eq. 5-6) is introduced via a loosely justified FLOPs-equalization heuristic rather than a formal derivation, making the "theoretical" framing somewhat overstated relative to what is actually proven.

The headline efficiency numbers (2.3x speedup, 19.7 FPS) rely heavily on FP8 quantization and LightVAE, which are not contributions of this paper; the sparse-attention method alone yields a much more modest 1.2-1.3x end-to-end speedup, so the significance of the core contribution is somewhat inflated by combining with orthogonal techniques.

Sparsity ratios are not matched consistently across baselines (static methods ~80%, dynamic methods ~90%, Light Forcing's own effective sparsity is chunk-dependent and starts at 0% for chunk 1), which complicates a strictly fair, apples-to-apples comparison of quality-vs-compute trade-offs.

Evaluation is restricted to 1.3B-parameter models only (acknowledged as a limitation); no evidence is given for how CAG/HSA scale to larger, production-grade models (e.g., 14B), which is important given the claimed practical relevance for real-time deployment.

Ablation results show large, somewhat erratic swings in the Dynamic Degree metric across settings (63.1 → 37.5 → 66.7 in Table 2), and no repeated trials, variance, or confidence intervals are reported anywhere in the paper, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported gains, especially given VBench metrics are known to be sensitive to seed/prompt sampling.
Design choices such as always keeping the first chunk dense are stated but not ablated, so their individual contribution to the reported quality gains is unclear.
Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis is limited to top-k in HSA; other key hyperparameters (sbase, starget, chunk size dependency) are fixed without exploration or justification of robustness.

Code is only promised for future release, and several implementation details (e.g., exact schedule of sparsity ratios per chunk beyond Radial Attention's baseline) are only partially specified, which somewhat limits reproducibility at submission time.

strengths: Novel problem framing: identifies and empirically demonstrates why sparse attention methods designed for bidirectional video diffusion fail when naively applied to autoregressive (AR) models (error accumulation across chunks, insufficient historical context utilization), supported by clear toy experiments (Fig. 2) and attention pattern visualizations (Fig. 4).

Two complementary technical contributions (Chunk-Aware Growth for adaptive per-chunk sparsity allocation, and Hierarchical Sparse Attention for coarse-to-fine frame/block selection) that are well-motivated by the empirical observations and target distinct failure modes.

Extensive and diverse experimental validation across three different AR video models (Self Forcing, LongLive, Infinite-Forcing), two benchmarks (VBench, VBench-Long), and comparisons against six sparse-attention baselines plus feature-caching/token-reduction methods (TeaCache, DyCoke).

Strong empirical results: the method frequently matches or exceeds dense-attention quality while providing consistent speedups, and qualitative examples convincingly show fewer artifacts (duplication, over-saturation, color drift) compared to baselines.

Thorough ablations (component-wise, hyperparameter sensitivity on top-k) and engineering-level deployment analysis (multi-GPU latency, peak memory, FP8/kernel fusion/LightVAE integration) that demonstrate practical real-time feasibility (e.g., 27.4 FPS on RTX 5090).
Reasonably transparent limitations section acknowledging model-scale restriction, remaining artifacts, and GPU-specific kernel tuning issues.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation of Chunk-Aware Growth (Appendix C) largely reuses a generic diffusion-model TV-distance bound from prior work (Li et al., 2023); the translation of this bound into the concrete sparsity allocation formula (Eq. 5) and its FLOPs-matching solution (Eq. 6) is heuristic rather than rigorously derived, and constants C1, C2 remain unspecified, weakening the claimed theoretical grounding.

The core algorithmic contribution alone yields relatively modest end-to-end speedups (1.19x-1.3x); the headline 2.0-3.0x and FPS numbers are driven largely by orthogonal engineering optimizations (FP8 quantization, kernel fusion, LightVAE) that are not novel contributions of this paper, which could overstate the method's own impact if not read carefully.

Ablations reveal that CAG alone substantially hurts Dynamic Degree (63.1 -> 37.5 in Table 3), indicating a real trade-off/limitation of the sparsity-allocation strategy that is only compensated by adding HSA; this interaction is not deeply analyzed or theoretically explained.

Quality gains over dense attention are inconsistent across metrics (e.g., Semantic Score is sometimes lower than dense baseline, such as 80.9 vs 81.2 for Self-Forcing), so the claim of near-lossless or superior performance is only partially supported.
Evaluation is restricted to 1.3B-parameter models; no experiments at larger scale are provided to substantiate generality, which the authors themselves note as a limitation.

Sparsity ratios are set differently across baseline categories (~80% static vs ~90% dynamic) for comparison, and while justified, this could still affect the fairness of direct quality/latency comparisons.
Evaluation relies entirely on automated VBench metrics without human perceptual studies, which may not fully capture subjective video quality differences highlighted in the qualitative figures.
The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with dual-use or misuse risks specific to accelerated, real-time video generation (e.g., deepfakes, disinformation).
